scores.rationale: Two snippets directly bear on the stylized fact. Snippet [9] explicitly states 'Decrease in DO may decrease the gonado-somatic index' citing multiple studies (Cheung et al. 2008a; Landry et al. 2007; Long et al. 2013a; Thomas et al. 2006; Wu et al. 2003), and snippet [17] independently affirms that 'hypoxia can reduce gonadosomatic index and gonad development in fish' citing several of the same sources. No snippet contradicts the fact. The remaining snippets merely discuss GSI in non-hypoxia contexts (reproduction modeling, byssus allocation, DEB parameterization) and are topically related but do not bear on the DO–GSI relationship. The two supporting snippets cite a consistent body of primary literature, giving moderate, internally consistent support with no conflict, hence corroborated direction but only moderate strength since the evidence within this corpus stems largely from review-style restatements of the same underlying references.

While most snippets discuss GSI in various species, they relate to seasonal cycles, hormonal treatments, sex differences, and energy allocation during reproduction—none manipulate or observe the effect of oxygen levels on GSI. There is no evidence either supporting or contradicting the stylized fact that decreased DO may decrease the gonado-somatic index. Evidence is essentially absent, so the corpus provides insufficient basis to judge the claim.
